transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-11
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Stratus - Head of ML), Tom Becker (Stratus - Infra), Riya Patel (Stratus - SRE)

Summary (auto): Discussed latency/throughput targets, deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private), benchmarking plan, and security/compliance needs. Next steps captured.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood. Maya our SE is here as well. quick round robin?
[00:05] Lena (Stratus): Hi, Lena. We're excited, thanks. we— uh— we run a real-time summarization feature in our product, has to be very low latency for the customer-facing UI.
[00:12] Tom (Stratus): Tom here, infra. mainly I'll be listening for throughput numbers and what implies for our cloud spend.
[00:18] Riya (Stratus): Riya, SRE. focused on p95 and tail latencies, and on how graceful degradation works.
[00:24] Maya (Redwood SE): great, thanks. quick agenda: confirm target p95 & concurrency, discuss streaming behavior, token/sec baseline, and then map hosted vs dedicated vs private options.
[00:34] Jordan: can you share current targets?
[00:37] Lena: sure. our soft target is p95 under 200 milliseconds for short completions (~20-60 tokens). for longer streaming replies (300–800 tokens) we need the first-token p95 under 250ms and sustained streaming throughput so the UI feels continuous.
[00:49] Maya: ok, that's helpful. also are you doing synchronous single-turn calls or multi-turn chat with KV cache reuse?
[00:55] Lena: mostly single-turn summarization but we do prefix caching for some workflows; so KV cache behavior matters for warm vs cold starts.
[01:03] Tom: concurrency-wise we see steady-state of 40–60 concurrent requests, with bursts up to ~200 for peak marketing events.
[01:11] Jordan: good. so p95 200ms for short tokens, concurrency steady 40–60, burst 200. streaming for long outputs. got it.
[01:18] Maya: i'll run through what we typically measure: token/sec on different model variants and hardware, latency p50/p95/p99, batch sizing effects, and streaming head-of-line latency. we also look at warm-path vs cold-path with KV cache and model quantization differences.
[01:29] Lena: we have a constraint around cost — we prefer hosted if it meets targets, otherwise dedicated capacity. private (VPC/on-prem) is for regulated customers only but we want the option.
[01:38] Jordan: that matches what we usually see. quick callouts: hosted is easiest to get started and has dynamic scaling; dedicated gives predictable throughput and often better tail latencies due to reserved pools; private adds network control and KMS/HSM integration but has a longer provisioning time.
[01:50] Tom: on tails — how do you handle fallbacks when a requested instance is saturated? we can't accept large tail spikes.
[01:56] Maya: several layers: smart routing to less-loaded model variants, graceful degradation to lower-token models, and autoscaling with burst capacity. for p95 specifically we tune batching and instance assignment to keep tail low. also prefix/KV cache reduces token work on warm requests.
[02:10] Riya: when you say model variants, do you mean different quantizations or smaller architectures? need to understand accuracy tradeoffs.
[02:16] Maya: both. often we run a high-accuracy float model for serving, with an int8 quantized variant as fallback. quality monitoring flags regressions and can trigger rollbacks.
[02:25] Lena: ok. can you give us some ballpark throughput numbers? for example tokens per second and latency for a 20-50 token response on hosted vs dedicated?
[02:33] Maya: ballpark: on a modern A100/H100-class instance, unconstrained single-request latency for 20–50 tokens is often in the 60–150ms p95 range for optimized kernels and small batch sizes. token/sec raw throughput depends on batching: with batching and continuous serving we commonly see effective 1000–30000 tokens/sec per GPU for medium-sized models; smaller models or quantized variants can do more. these are rough — we should run your prompts to confirm.
[02:58] Tom: that's a wide range. for budgeting we need more deterministic numbers.
[03:02] Jordan: agreed. that's why we propose a benchmark run using your real prompt set and expected concurrency profile. we'll run hosted simulation and dedicated reserved pool and compare p95s and token/sec at 40/60/200 concurrency.
[03:13] Lena: what's involved for the benchmark?
[03:15] Maya: we'll need sample prompts, expected token lengths, desired success criteria (p95 thresholds), and a list of models you want to test. we provide a benchmark harness and a spreadsheet with results — we'll include latency distributions, token/sec, and cost per 1M tokens.
[03:28] Riya: do you support streaming in the benchmark? we need first-byte latency and sustained token emission rates.
[03:33] Maya: yes, we exercise streaming mode. we measure first-byte p95 and tokens/sec during streaming. also measure head-of-line latency when multiple streams are multiplexed.
[03:41] Tom: about network: if we go private VPC, do you route inside the customer's subnet or is there a managed connector?
[03:47] Jordan: for VPC we support private control plane with customer-managed networking; options include VPC peering, PrivateLink-style connectors, or an on-prem package. we'll include networking options in the follow-up doc.
[03:58] Lena: security is important. do you have SOC 2? KMS support? audit logs?
[04:02] Jordan: yes SOC 2 Type II. KMS integrations for customer-managed keys, RBAC, SSO/SAML. we can share our security whitepaper and SOC2 report after an NDA.
[04:11] Riya: for the dedicated case, how isolated are GPU pools? can we reserve a specific fleet?
[04:15] Maya: dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and capacity guarantees; you can configure autoscaling and burst policies. SLA covers uptime and target latencies for your committed capacity.
[04:24] Lena: latency vs cost tradeoffs — do you have guidance on batching and tokenization to hit p95 <200ms?
[04:30] Maya: yes. for short responses, keep batch sizes small (1–8) to reduce head-of-line. continuous batching helps token/sec but raises tail. autoscaling thresholds and dynamic batching rules help keep p95 low while preserving throughput. quantized models reduce compute time per token but may affect quality.
[04:44] Tom: anything about prefix cache warming? our traffic has some repeated prefixes.
[04:48] Maya: prefix/KV cache is good — warm cache reduces per-request compute significantly. our runtime supports KV cache reuse across requests when prompts share prefixes or contexts. benchmark will include cold vs warm scenarios.
[04:58] Lena: regarding metrics: we want p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens.
[05:04] Jordan: noted — we'll include those.
[05:07] Riya: question about burst to 200 concurrency: do you rely on overprovisioning for that or can hosted auto-scale quickly enough?
[05:13] Maya: hosted can autoscale but very sudden spikes can hit cold starts. we recommend a reserved burst pool for critical events (hosted can be configured with burst capacity) or dedicated capacity with scaled headroom. for strict SLOs, dedicated is more predictable.
[05:26] Tom: in terms of token/sec benchmarks — are measurements affected by network egress for streaming?
[05:31] Maya: streamed tokens are subject to network latency for first byte and sustained throughput; we measure both. in practice network adds a small constant overhead compared to compute when you're on low-latency networks; for global clients region placement matters.
[05:44] Lena: any gotchas around model compilation/kernels for our prompt lengths? we get longer context windows (3k–8k tokens) sometimes.
[05:50] Maya: longer contexts increase KV cache and memory usage; compilation chooses kernels accordingly. sequence length distribution affects batch sizing and memory headroom — we'll include guidance based on your exact distribution.
[06:01] Jordan: can we run a small example now? maybe quick rough calc: if we need p95 200ms at 50 concurrent short requests, what's the likely capacity?
[06:08] Maya: rough back-of-envelope: assume 150ms p95 per request when concurrency per GPU is 8–16 depending on model; so for 50 concurrent you'd need ~4–6 GPUs for consistent p95, plus headroom for bursts. again depends on model and batching.
[06:24] Tom: that's useful; cost numbers help.
[06:26] Jordan: we'll include cost per 1M tokens in the spreadsheet and model-specific throughput.
[06:32] Lena: one more: are function/tool-calling or structured outputs supported? we sometimes do tool-calling which changes token patterns.
[06:39] Maya: yes, supported; benchmarks will include tool-calling patterns. streaming with tool calls can add latency when model decides to call out — we track that in the harness.
[06:49] Riya: how do you validate accuracy regression when using quantized fallbacks?
[06:53] Maya: we link quality monitoring to prompt sets and eval suites. if quantized variant drifts beyond a threshold we mark it as not eligible as fallback. you can set thresholds.
[07:03] Jordan: ok, let's capture next steps. we'll run the benchmark with your sample prompts. Maya will send the benchmark plan and what artifacts we need. Jordan will send pricing doc and hosted/dedicated comparison. Riya will share prompt set and concurrency patterns.
[07:13] Lena: yep. ideally we'd see a simple hosted baseline first then dedicated numbers.
[07:17] Tom: and can you include a proof-of-concept offer for a short dedicated pilot (2–4 weeks)?
[07:22] Jordan: yes we can propose a pilot. we'll include pilot terms in the follow-up.
[07:26] Maya: quick note on measurement specifics we'll include: for streaming we'll report first-byte p95, median token emission rate, and end-to-end time to N tokens. for non-streaming p95 we'll run at target concurrency and report distribution.
[07:39] Riya: for the benchmark infrastructure who runs the loadgen? you or us?
[07:42] Maya: we can run the harness and invite you to monitor live, or we can provide the harness for you to run in your environment. for private deployments you'll run it on your infra with our agent.
[07:53] Lena: good. any concerns about data residency? some of our customers require EU-only data.
[07:57] Jordan: we have region controls and private deployments; for EU-only we can set up region-restricted hosting or private. will include options.
[08:05] Tom: do you support customer-managed KMS for on-hosted flows?
[08:09] Jordan: yes — customer-managed keys via KMS, HSM options for private.
[08:13] Maya: also we'll attach audit log examples in the security pack.
[08:18] Lena: ok thanks.
[08:20] Jordan: any final questions?
[08:22] Riya: just to confirm the benchmark will include warm/cold KV cache comparison and streaming first-byte metrics, right?
[08:27] Maya: yes.
[08:29] Lena: we'll aim to share prompt set by end of day tomorrow.
[08:33] Jordan: perfect. we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and pricing.
[08:36] Tom: great, thanks.
[08:38] Jordan: recap — next steps: Jordan send pricing and pilot terms; Maya send benchmark plan; Riya/Lena share prompts and concurrency profile; schedule 2-hour benchmark window.
[08:48] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and update CRM. bye.
